newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian jobs data confuses rate outlook.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian jobs data confuses rate outlook.

text.p: Australian December employment data released on Wednesday added more confusion than clarity to the interest rate outlook, with analysts finding signs of both strength and weakness in the figures.
The headline figures for the month were a 4,500 rise in employment and an unemployment rate of 8.6 percent. The results were exactly in line with market expectations.
Some analysts said the data not only supported the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decision to cut interest rates, but suggested there could be room for further rate cuts in 1997.
Westpac Banking Corp senior economist John Peters said the data highlighted ongoing labour market weakness on the back of easing economic growth.
"The data also reinforces just why the RBA moved to ease rates three times in late 1996 and why the prospects are very good for another official rate cut in early 1997," Peters said.
But others disagreed, pointing to the fact that while employment growth was soft in December and the jobless rate was up slightly, employment rose by 54,500 over the December quarter.
That translated to average growth of just over 18,000, above the 10,000 to 15,000 jobs growth economists see as necessary to keep the unemployment rate steady.

"It's not as weak as perhaps people might have thought because when you put it all together you've had three months now which have generated 55,000 jobs," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said. "Obviously we need more than 4,500 (jobs) a month to get the unemployment rate to come down ...", he said, adding that this was likely as they economy picked up in 1997.

Roberts felt the data argued against the need for a rate cut, but others said that while growth of between 15,000 and 20,000 would see modest progress in lowering the unemployment rate and allow the government's labour market forecasts to be met, it would not definitely rule out another rate cut.

"The inflation outlook remains benign and there may be scope in the current environment of sub potential growth for the RBA to give the economy a further nudge along," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.

Adding to the confusion over how to interpret the data, the Australian Bureau of Statistics confirmed a Reuters report in December that a new telephone survey method introduced in August had been underestimating monthly jobs growth by 6,000 to 9,000 a month. Effectively it meant the 58,300 jobs growth reported in the five months since August would have been between 30,000 and 45,000 thousand higher if the old survey system had been used.

"Employment growth on a year-to basis, while not stellar, is clearly doing better, and the unemployment rate is 'flat to down' rather than 'flat to up'", Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said of the distortion to the data.
"We can now be far more confident that the labour market is, at the least, not deteriorating," he said.

If the labour market was not deteriorating, then that should temper some of the calls for a near term easing by the RBA, at least until the impact of the three rate cuts in the second half of 1996 had been seen, some analysts felt.

"In the grand scheme of things the bias (of the new survey method) is not large, but is supportive of the view that the RBA should not be rushed into easing by fears that the economy has stalled," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Tony Meer said.
